messages.author: 28fb4771522c5139
messages.subject: Functions that operates on groups.
parts:
Hi Hadley,

Absolutely fantastic package. Thanks a lot.

There is an interesting feature in vline and hline geoms. A custom
function is allowed to be passed as argument in the "intercept" setting.
This function operates within groups. Apparently this is not documented
anywhere in the book.

I would find it very helpful if unevaluated functions were allowed in
other geoms and aesthetics as well (in settings not mappings).
Something like:
geom_point(aes(x=cyl),y=.(mean(mpg))), or
geom_point(aes(x=cyl),y=.(mean(mpg)),colour=.(myfunc(mpg,gear))) ,

mean and myfunc above would operate on groups (as oppose to functions in
aes(...) which apply to whole data.frame).


Many thanks,
Vitalie.

It's in the documentation though - and that's where you'll need to
look to find small things like this. It's also a feature I'm somewhat
ambivalent about, so I don't want to publicise it too much, in case I
later decide it was a bad idea.

> I would find it very helpful if unevaluated functions were allowed in
> other geoms and aesthetics as well (in settings not mappings).
> Something like:
> geom_point(aes(x=cyl),y=.(mean(mpg))), or
> geom_point(aes(x=cyl),y=.(mean(mpg)),colour=.(myfunc(mpg,gear))) ,
>
> mean and myfunc above would operate on groups (as oppose to functions in
> aes(...) which apply to whole data.frame).

It's so easy to do that outside of ggplot2, that I don't think it's
worth adding:

mtcars2 <- ddply(mtcars, .(cyl), transform, mean_mpg = mean(mpg))
qplot(wt, mean_mpg, data = mtcars2)

ddply comes from my plyr package (http://had.co.nz/plyr), or you could
use ave() from base R.

This way you have much much much much more flexibility in the way that
you manipulate the data. I'm working on a chapter for the book on
just this topic.

Regards,

Hadley

I also was thinking that way (plyr is my routine tool since it's
appearance- great idea!) but felt somewhat uneasy about efficiency.
Since, instead of one point (mean(mpg)) hundreds of overlapping points for
each group are plotted (don't they?).
And beside that lazy folks like me are always reluctant in adding
additional columns to data.frames that already have several dozens (and
additionally thinking of new names, additional lines in code and all that
stuff:(...)

Incidentally, plyr uses very nice naming conventions. Shouldn't reshape
follow the example? String and formula interfaces in melt and cast are
somewhat awkward respectively for interactive and programmatic use. Plyr's
interchangeable .(), c() interfaces are just a bless for all purposes.

All the best!!
Vitally.

Well presumably you'd do something different in a real situation, maybe:

mtmean <- ddply(mtcars, .(cyl), colwise(mean))

> And beside that lazy folks like me are always reluctant in adding additional
> columns to data.frames that already have several dozens (and additionally
> thinking of new names, additional lines in code and all that stuff:(...)

I understand your point, but at some point in the process those
variables have to be created, and if it's all done with in ggplot, I
have to make an already complicated process even more complicated to
deal with all the special cases, not to mention harder to describe and
understand. So I'm symapthetic, but I'd rather solve the problem
outside of ggplot, rather than inside.

> Incidentally, plyr uses very nice naming conventions. Shouldn't reshape
> follow the example? String and formula interfaces in melt and cast are
> somewhat awkward respectively for interactive and programmatic use. Plyr's
> interchangeable .(), c() interfaces are just a bless for all purposes.

I have a half rewritten version of reshape that does use them (as well
as supporting the old format), and is also 5-20x times faster
depending on the reshape. Unfortunately, it doesn't cover all the
possible reshape outputs and I haven't had time to work on it for a
while.
